value.overview: The Hermit Warbler is a small New World warbler of western North America. It breeds mainly in mature coniferous forests of the Pacific Northwest and California, then migrates south for winter. Its name comes from its preference for forest habitats rather than from solitary behavior. Adult males are strongly marked with a yellow face and throat, black crown and cheek, and gray back, while females and immature birds are duller. The species is a regular migrant and winter visitor in parts of Central America, including Costa Rica.
value.classification: The Hermit Warbler belongs to the family Parulidae, the wood-warblers, and the genus Setophaga. Its scientific name is Setophaga occidentalis.
value.identification: This small warbler is about 12–13 cm long. The adult male has a bright yellow face and throat, a black crown and cheek patch, a dark eye line, gray upperparts, and white underparts with some black streaking on the sides. Females and immature birds are less sharply marked, with olive-gray upperparts and a paler yellow face. In Costa Rica, identification can be difficult because other migrant warblers may also show yellow facial markings. Its active movements through foliage and thin, sharp call notes are useful supporting clues.
value.rangeHabitat: The Hermit Warbler breeds in western North America, especially in mature coniferous forests from Washington and Oregon south through California and into parts of the southwestern United States. During the nonbreeding season it occurs from western Mexico through Central America. In Costa Rica it is an uncommon migrant and winter visitor, recorded mainly in forested highlands and other wooded areas, including montane habitats and forest edges. It generally favors trees and dense vegetation rather than open agricultural land.
value.migrationStatus: The species is migratory. Birds breeding in the western United States and Canada move south after breeding, and some reach Costa Rica during migration or the northern winter. In Costa Rica it is not a resident breeder; records are seasonal and comparatively uncommon.
value.breeding: Hermit Warblers usually breed in mature coniferous forests, often in tall trees with relatively open trunks and a developed canopy. The female builds a small cup nest, commonly placed on a horizontal branch or in dense foliage. The clutch generally contains several eggs, which are incubated by the female. Both adults feed the young. Breeding timing varies geographically but is concentrated in late spring and summer in the northern part of the range.
value.dietFeeding: The Hermit Warbler feeds mainly on insects and other small arthropods, including caterpillars, beetles, ants, wasps, and spiders. It usually searches methodically among conifer needles and branches, picking prey from foliage or making short flights to capture insects. During migration and winter it may also take small fruits or other plant foods when available, but animal prey remains its principal food.
value.behavior: This warbler is active and often difficult to see as it moves through the upper and middle levels of trees. It commonly forages alone or in mixed-species flocks with other small insect-eating birds outside the breeding season. Males sing from elevated branches during the breeding season, while both sexes give short call notes during movement and foraging. It may remain quiet and inconspicuous in Costa Rica, especially in dense montane vegetation.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be declining, although the species remains widespread and numerous enough to be assessed as Least Concern.
conservation.threats: Loss, degradation, and fragmentation of mature coniferous forests affect breeding habitat, while forest conversion and degradation in parts of the migration and wintering range may reduce habitat quality. Climate change may alter forest composition, insect availability, and the timing of migration and breeding.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore mature forests across the species’ breeding, migration, and wintering ranges. In Costa Rica, conserving montane and other forested habitats used by migratory birds is beneficial. Reducing pesticide use, supporting bird-friendly shade and native vegetation, and keeping cats indoors can also reduce risks to insect-eating migratory birds.
